articles.title: House Dems overwhelmingly reject anti-socialism resolution after 2 moderates defy Jeffries
articles.summary: House Democrats were split on a vote to condemn socialism after two Democrats helped Republicans push their agenda forward.
articles.body: The House of Representatives passed a resolution condemning socialism on Tuesday evening, with all but eight House Democrats voting against it. The resolution passed 220 to 192 with all "no" votes coming from the left, including Democrats’ senior leaders: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif. The legislation also affirmed support for election integrity and called for passage of the Safeguarding American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which nearly all Democrats oppose. In a stunning twist of fate, however, the vote would not have occurred if two House Democrats hadn't stepped in hours earlier to help the GOP through a procedural hurdle — blindsiding Jeffries in the process. JOHNSON SCORES WIN AS CONSERVATIVE REBELS END HOUSE FLOOR BLOCKADE OVER VOTER ID BILL House conservatives had threatened to tank a procedural vote, called a "rule vote," meant to unlock debate on several bills GOP leaders wanted lawmakers to vote on this week. That included the resolution condemning socialism and several other unrelated bills. Five Republicans voted against the rule, which was poised to fail until Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., provided two critical votes to get the GOP over the finish line in a narrow 209 to 208 vote. All Republicans wound up voting in favor of the resolution condemning socialism and affirming election integrity on Tuesday evening, however. TENSIONS ERUPT IN HOUSE HEARING AS GOP ADVANCES ANTI-SOCIALISM RESOLUTION WHILE DEMS RAGE: 'SILLY SEASON' Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez were among the Democrats who joined the GOP in that vote, as well as Reps. Don Davis, D-N.C., Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas, Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, Kathy Castor, D-Fla., Gabe Vasquez, D-N.M., and Darren Soto, D-Fla. Reps. Maggie Goodlander, D-N.H., and Chrissy Houlahan, D-Pa., voted "present." Socialism has dominated the 2026 midterm election season on both sides of the aisle. Democrats are grappling with a far-left insurgency within their ranks as candidates linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) continue to topple incumbents and establishment-backed candidates across the country. It's provided fodder for the House GOP while it fights an uphill battle to keep control of Congress in November as Republicans warn the socialist left will take over the Democratic Party if it wins. "Socialism has failed everywhere it's been tried without exception. It's a dangerous ideology that creates misery for the very people it claims to help," Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "Today's vote puts the Left on the record and removes any doubt about where my colleagues on the other side of the aisle stand." Rep. Jeff Crank, R-Colo., who led the resolution, told Fox News Digital, "The resolution is pretty easy, right? It condemns socialism in all its forms, including the DSA, recommits ourselves to the Constitution of the United States…a third point is that we don't want non-citizens voting in elections." "They can certainly be critical, but it's just a quick choice for the American people to see where people stand on this stuff," Crank said. But Democrats contended that Republicans' largely symbolic resolution was a meaningless political exercise that does nothing to help Americans with their everyday problems. Many on the left have also dismissed the GOP's election integrity efforts as voter suppression. "So you're concerned about rising gas, or are you concerned about grocery prices? You know, don't worry. Republicans in Congress are passing another non-binding resolution condemning socialism," Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., said during a hearing on Monday. The Tuesday evening vote would not have been possible without Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez rescuing Republicans' agenda. Golden is not running for re-election, while Gluesenkamp Perez is one of the most vulnerable Democrats in the country. It's almost unheard of for the minority party to help their political rivals pass a rule, and Jeffries told reporters he was not notified beforehand. The five House Republicans who voted against it were Reps. Pete Sessions, R-Texas; Chip Roy, R-Texas; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., Clay Higgins, R-La.; and Andy Harris, R-Md. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The rebels' issue was not with the measure itself, nor the bills it would have allowed the House to pass. Their votes were a protest against how their leaders handled a plan to avert a government shutdown just before the midterm elections, a short-term funding bill called a continuing resolution (CR). That measure passed just before the rule vote began. But the five GOP lawmakers took issue with how the Senate modified an original House-passed CR, including adding an unrelated measure to delay a congressionally approved hemp product ban by 30 days and a provision curbing the Trump administration’s control over federal grants. It's worth noting that Golden is also co-lead of a bill aimed at pausing new federal restrictions on certain American lobster and crab fishing industries, which would have also been stalled if the rule failed.

articles.title: Ted Cruz shuts down Trump Supreme Court talk with a fiery 'not just no, but hell no'
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz told Sean Hannity his answer to a Supreme Court nomination from Trump would be "not just no, but hell no," despite his deep legal background.
articles.body: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has dismissed speculation about a potential Supreme Court nomination, saying his response to President Donald Trump would be "not just no, but hell no." Speaking on the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast, Cruz said he would rather remain in politics than serve on the Supreme Court. "So look, my answer is not just no, but hell no. And listen, I don't say that lightly. I mean, it’s a big deal. The court is an institution I revere," Cruz told Hannity. ALITO NOT EXPECTED TO RETIRE THIS TERM, COOLING SUPREME COURT VACANCY SPECULATION: SOURCES "And a lot of people are surprised, because I've spent an awful lot of my professional life around the court, in the court. And for so many people, it is their life dream to do," he added. Trump has floated Cruz’s name for the Supreme Court in the past, joking he’d be the only nominee to get "100% of the Democrat vote, 100% of the Republican vote" because lawmakers would want to "get him out" of Congress. TRUMP CHEERS ALITO STAYING FOR ANOTHER SUPREME COURT TERM: 'ONE OF THE GREATEST OF ALL TIME' Before entering politics, Cruz graduated from Princeton University and got his law degree from Harvard Law School. After law school, he clerked for Chief Justice William Rehnquist and later worked in private practice. During his conversation with Hannity, Cruz called Trump a "good friend," despite their rivalry during the 2016 Republican presidential primary. He also said that federal judges typically have to stay out of politics and policy battles. SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES "Because a principled federal judge stays out of politics and stays out of policy fights," Cruz said of why he would not want a seat on the bench. Cruz was sworn into the Senate in 2013. He previously served as solicitor general of Texas from 2003 to 2008 and argued nine cases before the U.S. Supreme Court. The Texas Tribune reported that Cruz was among 20 potential Supreme Court picks on Trump’s 2020 short list. Cruz responded to his inclusion on the list in a statement on X, then known as Twitter: "I am grateful for the president’s confidence in me and for his leadership in nominating principled constitutionalists to the federal bench over the last four years," Cruz said. "It’s humbling and an immense honor to be considered for the Supreme Court. The High Court plays a unique role in defending our Constitution, and there is no greater responsibility in public service than to support and defend the Constitution of the United States," he added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP At the time, Cruz said he had been "blessed to lead the fight to preserve our constitutional liberties" in the Senate and looked forward to continuing that work. Fox News's Alexandra Koch contributed to this report.

articles.title: The Alaska Senate race: 3 Republicans, 2 Dans Sullivan, 1 Democrat
articles.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola will be the only Democrat on the ballot after Democrat David Leslie, who finished fourth in the primary, withdrew.
articles.body: The Alaska Division of Elections on Tuesday named the four Senate candidates who will be on the ballot this fall in a closely watched race that will be decided by ranked-choice voting. Voters will make their selections among two Republicans named Dan Sullivan, another named Gerald Heikes and Democrat Mary Peltola, who finished first during the all-party primary in which the top four advance to the general election. Democrat David Leslie had finished fourth, but he withdrew from the race Monday. His withdrawal means fifth-place candidate Gerald Heikes, a Republican, will appear on the ballot. The race is considered one of the most competitive in the 2026 cycle and a potential pickup for Democrats, who are hoping to gain control of the Senate. It’s made headlines due to the novelty of having two candidates with the same first and last name. Dan J. Sullivan, a former schoolteacher who came in third in the primary, is seeking to unseat Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. But his candidacy has faced legal challenges from the senator and other Republicans who allege he is working with Peltola, a former congresswoman, and entered the race as a potential spoiler. He and Peltola have denied any coordination with each other, as have their campaigns. Although the Alaska Supreme Court allowed Sullivan to stay on the ballot after originally being disqualified by the Division of Elections, state and federal authorities are conducting their own investigation into his campaign. The Division of Elections on Tuesday also named general election candidates for the governor’s contest, including Republicans Dave Bronson and Bernadette Wilson and Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the top finisher in the primary. They are running to replace term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy. Tom Begich, a Democrat who finished second in the primary, withdrew from the race before Tuesday.

articles.title: Key Texas county votes to cut polling sites ahead of the midterms
articles.summary: Officials in Tarrant County, the third most-populous in Texas, approved a plan to reduce the number of polling locations by 92 compared to the 2022 elections.
articles.body: Officials in Texas’ third-largest county voted Tuesday to significantly reduce the number of polling sites for this fall’s midterm elections, drawing protests from Democrats and voting rights advocates. Commissioners in Tarrant County, a fast-growing and politically competitive area that includes Fort Worth, approved a plan that results in 92 fewer Election Day polling locations compared with the 2022 midterms. The roughly 30% reduction leaves the county with 224 polling sites to serve 1.3 million voters. Voters in the county are able to cast ballots at any of those polling sites. The three Republicans on the Tarrant County Commissioners Court voted for their plan, while the two Democrats voted against it. Research has found that each additional minute of travel time to a polling location can affect voter participation. The NAACP, the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas and other groups said in a letter that the changes would hit voters of color hardest because many of the reductions are in majority-minority areas in Fort Worth and Arlington. Supporters of the plan say that it will save money and that there are more than enough options for people to vote. The move comes amid a critical Senate contest in Texas, with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico taking on state Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican. Talarico urged the county to reject the plan ahead of Tuesday’s vote. “The most powerful people in this county, the most powerful people in this country, don’t want us to be able to vote easily,” Talarico told reporters Sunday, according to The Associated Press. Tarrant County has emerged as a key political battleground in Texas. President Donald Trump won it in the 2024 presidential race after Joe Biden flipped it four years prior. And Democrats Beto O’Rourke and Colin Allred narrowly carried the county in the 2018 and 2024 Senate races, respectively, even as they both went on to lose. Texas law gives counties the power to decide how many polling sites they use. And some counties have begun using fewer sites as they have moved to countywide voting in recent years. Dozens of voters urged the commissioners to vote against the cuts. Some criticized the elimination of specific polling places — like one at the University of Texas at Arlington — while others noted that the county has experienced significant population growth and voter participation in recent years. “The right to vote is the bedrock of our democracy,” said a woman named Linda Northern. “This will make it harder for brown, Black and low-income voters to have the same right to vote as you do. This is wrong.” Tarrant County Commissioner Roderick Miles Jr., a Democrat, added ahead of the vote, “This is about ensuring that the rights that people bled and died for are accessible to everybody.” Tarrant County Judge Tim O’Hare, a Republican on the commissioner court, argued that Miles wanted more polling sites in his area. “There’s no argument to that that you can come up with other than you want to be able to have more in your precinct,” O’Hare said. A handful of speakers supported the plan, noting that some sites were used by few voters and required a significant number of poll workers and financial resources. “I support the proposition that’s in front of us as far as reducing the number of voting sites. I’ve been a poll watcher, a poll worker, a precinct chair and all those things, and when you vote, when you go to a poll place that had 34 people all day long, you think this is kind of a waste of resources,” said one speaker, who did not identify herself.

articles.title: Former Florida governor hopeful hauled out of county meeting after protesting Israel investments
articles.summary: James Fischback was forcibly removed from a Miami-Dade commissioners meeting after protesting the county's raised investment limit in Israel bonds.
articles.body: James Fischback, a former Florida gubernatorial candidate and controversial political figure, was forcibly removed from a Miami-Dade Board of County Commissioners meeting Tuesday afternoon after protesting the county's expanded investment in Israel-backed bonds. "Do you serve the people of Hialeah or of Haifa? Do you serve the people of Aventura or of Tel Aviv? Do you serve the people of South Miami or of Jerusalem? This money should be invested here in this community. It should be invested in Miami-Dade County," he added before officers escorted him from the room. The confrontation comes after the county voted earlier this summer to raise its investment cap with Israel from 3% to 5% of its portfolio — a move that allows it invest upwards of about $400 million to $450 million. The change has drawn opposition from figures like Fischback critical of using public funds to invest in Israel as the war in Gaza continues to fuel political divisions in the U.S. It has also provided Fischback a platform to continue his opposition to U.S.-Israel ties. ANTISEMITISM FIGHT EXPLODES IN FLORIDA AS VOTERS HEAD TO THE POLLS: 'POLITICAL POGROM' "What this is about, very simply, is whom do you serve?" Fischback said. Fischback, a Republican, has garnered national attention for his views on race and has developed a reputation for confrontational public appearances. Fischback was among the 11 GOP candidates seeking to replace outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis. He garnered 10.4% of the vote in the Aug. 18 primary but drew national attention for a series of inflammatory on-camera moments. In one such case, he repeatedly called Rep. Byron Donalds, the frontrunner, eventual nominee and one of the only Black Republicans in Congress, a "slave" repeatedly at a news conference. "Byron Donalds is a slave. I’m sorry, he’s a slave. He is a slave to his donors. He is a slave to the corporate interests, to the tech bros that want to turn our state into, in his own words, a financial capital," Fischback said. He would later shout a similar phrase at Donalds directly, catching Donalds on the way back to his car with a megaphone and a throng of supporters. "You’re a DEI hire. You’re a slave. Go back to New York," Fischback yelled. JOSH SHAPIRO WARNS THAT ATTACKS ON AIPAC ARE BEING USED TO 'SILENCE CERTAIN VOTERS' Fischback's comments on Tuesday weren't the only ones that expressed outrage over the portfolio change. Other members of the public who expressed concern about the change voiced disappointment that the county would put public investment dollars behind Israel, given the politically charged atmosphere around the topic of its relations with the U.S. Another woman who identified herself as Ivar Fandel walked to the podium wearing a "let Gaza live" shirt. "Item 5B does exist in the context of a budget crisis as well as a genocide against Palestinians in Gaza at the hands of Israel," Fandel said, referring to the agenda item discussing the county's change. During his campaign, Fischback positioned himself as one of the only Republican candidates to decline contributions from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). He also pledged to divest from Israel-backed bonds. "Florida has a specific policy. You’re not allowed to use taxpayer funds to buy foreign government bonds, with one exception: Israel. And so my premise is, first principles, we should not be lending taxpayer pensioner money to any foreign government," Fischback said in an interview with the American Conservative. He also blasted several candidates, including Donalds, for what he characterized as "singular allegiance" to Israel. HUCKABEE WARNS OF 'BIBLICAL IGNORANCE' AS HE DEFENDS CONSERVATIVE SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "I think people like Randy Fine and other AIPAC politicians have a singular allegiance. And that allegiance is to the best interests of Israel. The idea of saying ‘I am running to represent a foreign country’s interest in the United States Congress’ is preposterous. They’re buying allegiance," Fischback said in a post to X. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fischback did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Putin: German measures over Leipzig drone attack 'serious mistake'
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has called German punitive measures against Russia over a failed attack involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airpor...
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has called German punitive measures against Russia over a failed attack involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport a "serious mistake" and rejected Berlin's accusations against Moscow.

"Where is the evidence?" Putin asked at a press conference in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek. He dismissed evidence presented so far as "fabricated" and said the response by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government was primarily driven by domestic politics.

"Merz has lost the trust of citizens because he is not protecting Germany's national interests," Putin said following a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). He said the future of Germany's current political leadership would be at stake in upcoming elections due to the country's economic problems.

Germany on Tuesday said Russia was responsible for the failed attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said police investigations, patterns of criminal activity and intelligence findings pointed to Russian responsibility for the attempted attack.

A drone fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism was discovered on August 4 in the security zone of the airport, between Ukrainian cargo aircraft, prompting a temporary halt to flights.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced measures in response, including the closure of the Russian consulate general in Bonn on September 18 and the termination of the lease for the Russian House, a Russian cultural institution in the heart of Berlin.

articles.title: DOJ lawsuit targets alleged school ‘secret gender transitions’ policies that keep parents in the dark
articles.summary: The DOJ lawsuit against Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools alleges 'secret' gender transition plans locked parents out, violating FERPA and PPRA.
articles.body: The Department of Justice (DOJ) is investigating other school districts and contemplating additional lawsuits over alleged violations of federal parental rights laws, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon told Fox News Digital on Tuesday, calling the DOJ's newly filed "first-of-its-kind" case against Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools the "first of many." The DOJ sued Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools, aka KCKPS, on Tuesday, alleging the district violated the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA) with a district policy that facilitates "secret gender transitions" for students at school without their parents’ knowledge or consent. "No, we're not waiting. What we do is we ask for documents, we investigate, and then we try to resolve cases with school districts. And if we cannot, then we file lawsuits. And so there are many other lawsuits contemplated here and other investigations that are ongoing," Dhillon said when asked whether DOJ would wait for the Kansas case to conclude before pursuing other districts. Dhillon declined to identify the other districts under investigation, saying she did not want to prejudge the outcomes. EXCLUSIVE: HOUSE COMMITTEE PROBES CHICAGO PUBLIC SCHOOLS OVER HIDING 'GENDER AFFIRMATION' FROM PARENTS "This is a really important lawsuit for us. And the point I wanted to emphasize is that it's the first of many," she said. The DOJ lawsuit against KCKPS centers on internal guidance for transgender and gender non-conforming students. DOJ alleges the district has used versions of the guidance since 2017. Under the guidance described in the complaint, students can ask that their parents be excluded from school planning meetings and that their transgender or gender non-conforming status not be disclosed to them. The resulting written plans can address names, pronouns, school records, restroom and locker room use, sports and other accommodations. Asked about KCKPS’ assertion that it complies with federal law, Dhillon rejected the district’s position. FIRST ON FOX: SCHOOL LIED, HID DAUGHTER'S GENDER TRANSITION UNDER DISTRICT POLICY, PARENTS ALLEGE "Well, I think you can get that from the complaint, but they had secret gender transition plans that locked parents out of knowing what was being asked of their children. So I obviously completely reject that," Dhillon said. KCKPS disputed DOJ’s allegations Tuesday in a news release. "Contrary to the allegations in the Complaint, the district maintains that it is in full compliance with FERPA and PPRA and is disappointed by the DOJ’s decision to file the lawsuit," the release read. The district said it would respond through the federal court process and would not comment further while the litigation is pending. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION THREATENS KANAS SCHOOL DISTRICT FUNDING OVER TRANSGEDNER STUDENT POLICY The DOJ argues the written plans constitute education records under FERPA, and that excluding parents can prevent them from exercising their rights to inspect and challenge those records. The government separately alleges the district violates PPRA by allowing students to participate in meetings and evaluations that can reveal sensitive information without prior written parental consent. The Department of Education opened a FERPA investigation into KCKPS in August 2025. The federal government advised the district on Aug. 12 that its guidance violated FERPA and PPRA, and the complaint states the government ultimately determined KCKPS would not voluntarily comply. DOJ is asking a federal court to declare the district’s practices unlawful and prohibit enforcement of the guidance or similar policies that violate FERPA or PPRA. Dhillon said DOJ intends to pursue potential violations elsewhere. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "But I want there to be a very clear message to every. School district in the United States. They are on notice that if they violate FERPA and PPRA, the United State's Department of Justice stands ready to protect the rights of parents and the rights to pupils to privacy, dignity, and parental rights in determining how children are educated in the united states," Dhillon said. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Kansas referred questions about the lawsuit to the DOJ’s Office of Public Affairs.

articles.title: CCJ do Senado pode votar nesta quarta a PEC da Segurança  | G1
articles.standfirst: Proposta é uma das quatro matérias consideradas prioritárias pelo Palácio do Planalto e busca endurecer o combate ao crime organizado. Texto foi aprovado pela Câmara em março.
articles.summary: Proposta é uma das quatro matérias consideradas prioritárias pelo Palácio do Planalto e busca endurecer o combate ao crime organizado. Texto foi aprovado pela Câmara em março.
articles.body:
A Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública pode ser votada nesta quarta-feira (2) na Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) do Senado .

A proposta é uma das quatro matérias consideradas prioritárias pelo Palácio do Planalto e busca endurecer o combate ao crime organizado, ampliar instrumentos de enfrentamento às facções criminosas e alterar dispositivos constitucionais relacionados à segurança pública.

A proposta foi despachada para a CCJ do Senado após uma conversa entre o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), movimento interpretado por governistas como um sinal de retomada da tramitação de pautas de interesse do governo federal.

Essa possibilidade havia sido aprovada pelos deputados durante a tramitação da PEC. Segundo o senador, o financiamento dos dois fundos terá que ser feito posteriormente por lei ordinária.

Com a supressão, o texto não precisa retornar para a Câmara.

Se aprovada na CCJ, a PEC segue para o plenário do Senado. O governo trabalha para concluir a votação nesta quarta.

🔎 Para aprovar uma PEC é necessário o voto de 49 senadores em dois turnos.

A proposta estabelece na Constituição o 'Sistema Único de Segurança', que tem como objetivo integrar o combate ao crime organizado entre os entes.

Além disso, divide a responsabilidade sobre a segurança pública entre a União, Estados, Distrito Federal e municípios, bem como organização, garantias, direitos e deveres dos órgãos do sistema socioeducativo.

O projeto inclui na Constituição o Fundo Nacional de Segurança Pública e o Fundo Penitenciário Nacional. A União deverá repassar a Estados e municípios 50% de cada fundo.

CCJ do Senado durante reunião. — Foto: Saulo Cruz/Agência Senado

A proposta também atribui de forma expressa à Polícia Federal o combate a crimes cometidos por organizações e milícias privadas com repercussão interestadual ou internacional.

O texto inclui ainda polícias municipais no rol de órgãos responsáveis pela segurança pública.

Novas competências da União : competência privativa de legislar sobre "polícia federal e da polícia rodoviária federal" e "normas gerais da atividade de inteligência".

Crimes violentos : obrigatoriedade de prisão em estabelecimento penal estadual ou federal de segurança máxima ou de natureza especial; proibição ou restrição de progressão de regime, liberdade provisória, com ou sem fiança; restrição ou proibição de conversão de pena de prisão em outras medidas e concessão de saída temporária; expropriação de todo e qualquer bem, direito ou valor de conteúdo econômico envolvido com as atividades criminosas.

Competência da PRF : amplia a competência para atuação em hidrovias e ferrovias. Atualmente, o texto é restrito a rodovias. Também poderão atuar para exercer o policiamento ostensivo na proteção de bens, serviços e instalações federais e daqueles de interesse da União; prestar auxílio aos órgãos de segurança pública estaduais ou distritais, quando requerido por seus Governadores; atuar em cooperação com os demais órgãos integrantes do sistema único de segurança pública em estado de calamidade pública ou em caso de desastres.

Nova polícia : criação das polícias municipais comunitárias, organizadas em carreiras, para a realização de ações de policiamento ostensivo e comunitário, desde que o município atenda a critérios mínimos, como capacidade financeira.

articles.title: O que faz o senador? | G1
articles.standfirst: Senadores criam e alteram leis e têm funções exclusivas, como julgar impeachment e sabatinar indicados pelo Executivo. Série do g1 explica as eleições de 2026 e tira dúvidas.
articles.summary: Integrantes do Poder Legislativo, senadores dividem com a Câmara a função de criar, mudar ou revogar leis, além de ter funções próprias, como poder abrir processos de impeachment.
articles.body:
Senadores são representantes do Poder Legislativo nacional, papel similar ao desempenhado pelos deputados federais. A diferença está no número de integrantes para cada estado, com equidade dentro do Senado nacional e proporcional à população na Câmara, e parte das funções de cada Casa. O Senado possui atribuições específicas. Entenda no vídeo acima.

Cabe aos senadores criar, alterar ou revogar leis, fiscalizar o Poder Executivo, analisar o orçamento federal e pode criar Comissões Parlamentares de Inquérito (CPI) para investigar indícios de crimes.

Os senadores também podem abrir processo de impeachment contra o Presidente da República e são responsáveis por sabatinar os nomes indicados pelo chefe do Executivo a integrar o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), a Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) e outros cargos relevantes da República.

📍Em uma série de 50 vídeos, o g1 vai explicar os principais temas das eleições de 2026. Os conteúdos mostram como funcionam as pesquisas, explicam o papel dos cargos em disputa e o funcionamento do Congresso, e trazem orientações práticas para votar. A série também aborda o impacto das novas tecnologias na campanha, como inteligência artificial, deepfakes e influenciadores.

O g1 promove, nesta quarta-feira (2), debate com candidatos ao Senado por Pernambuco . Com mediação de Márcio Bonfim, o encontro, realizado em estúdio montado na redação da Globo no Recife, começa às 14h e será transmitido no site e nos perfis do portal no YouTube, TikTok e Instagram.

O programa marca a estreia da primeira série de debates realizados pelo g1 com candidatos à Câmara Alta. Depois de Pernambuco, estão marcados encontros nos estúdios da TV Globo no Rio de Janeiro São Paulo, Minas Gerais e Distrito Federal e nas afiliadas de Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Ceará e Piauí.

A série de debates integra a cobertura especial das Eleições 2026 realizada pela Globo. A iniciativa busca ampliar o espaço para a discussão de propostas e contribuir para que os eleitores conheçam os candidatos.

O debate com os candidatos ao Senado por Pernambuco poderá ser acompanhado pelo g1 e pelos perfis do portal nas redes sociais:

Foram chamados os candidatos de partidos e federações com representação mínima de cinco parlamentares no Congresso Nacional ou que alcançaram ao menos 5% de intenções de voto na última pesquisa Quaest ou Datafolha divulgada antes de cada debate.

Seis temas serão previamente definidos e comunicados às campanhas antes do debate. A ordem dos assuntos será sorteada antes do início do encontro.

Os candidatos poderão solicitar a palavra dentro das regras estabelecidas, com intervenções de até 1 minuto e 30 segundos por vez. Não serão permitidas intervenções consecutivas do mesmo candidato, que só poderá voltar a falar depois da manifestação de outro participante.

Ao final, todos terão direito a um minuto para as considerações finais.

Os pedidos de direito de resposta serão analisados pela produção e pelo mediador e poderão ser concedidos em casos de ofensa pessoal, conforme as regras previamente acordadas com as campanhas.

articles.title: Sen. Ed Markey defeats 47-year-old challenger to win Massachusetts Democratic Senate bid
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. Ed Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton in the Senate primary in Massachusetts, NBC News projects, in a victory for the party’s progressive wing.
articles.body: Democratic Sen. Ed Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton in the Senate primary in Massachusetts, NBC News projects, in a victory for the party’s progressive wing. Markey was winning about two-thirds of the vote percentage points with 69% of the expected vote reporting. See live results here Markey’s win comes as other longtime Democratic lawmakers have lost to younger challengers in primaries this year. But the 80-year-old senator fended off his challenger by touting his liberal record as an author of the Green New Deal and vocal supporter of “Medicare for All.” “It’s all about not just sending a Democrat to the Senate — it’s sending a progressive Democrat to the Senate from Massachusetts so there can be someone that reflects your values every single day,” Markey said at a rally on the eve of the primary, describing the race as “a progressive final round.” Moulton said Tuesday night that he had called Markey “to congratulate him on his victory tonight.” Moulton told supporters that Markey “has my full support as our Democratic nominee, and we must stand united this November to protect our democracy and defeat Donald Trump.” Moulton and his allies had a spending advantage in the race, spending $7.1 million on ads to Markey and his allies’ $3.9 million, according to AdImpact. That makes Markey’s win another victory for a progressive who faced an onslaught of well-funded attacks. On the campaign trail and the airwaves, Markey also touted endorsements from progressive leaders, including Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who both appeared in an ad for the senator, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. Moulton, the 47-year-old congressman, called in his campaign for generational change — a call that has cost a handful of House Democrats their seats in primaries across the country this year. Markey was first elected to the Senate in 2013 after serving nearly 40 years in the House. “Sen. Markey and I want the same things, but wanting isn’t winning, and the old way isn’t working,” Moulton said in one of his TV ads, listing policies including “tax the oligarchs, abolish ICE, pass healthcare for all.” But Markey and his allies attacked Moulton for his past criticism of liberal policies. Commonwealth Together PAC, an outside group that has attacked Moulton, launched an ad saying the congressman opposes Medicare for All and taxing billionaires, pointing to 2019 comments from Moulton’s unsuccessful campaign for president. Markey also sharply criticized Moulton on transgender issues, saying at the election-eve rally that Moulton “threw trans kids under the bus” after the 2024 election. Moulton told The New York Times after Democrats lost the presidential race: “I have two little girls. I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.” Moulton apologized to “anyone hurt by those comments” in a recent debate. In his primary campaign, Markey also vowed to continue fighting President Donald Trump. “It’s a moment in history where Trump is challenging everything that started right here 250 years ago,” Markey said in one ad, referring to the country’s founding. “We have a message from Massachusetts: We are going to fight.”

articles.title: Markey defeats Moulton in Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary
articles.summary: Sen. Ed Markey has fended off a challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton in the Massachusetts Democratic primary for Senate, Decision Desk HQ projects. Moulton, a 47-year-old who’s served in the House for six terms, had lodged a generational change campaign against Markey, an 80-year-old who served 20 terms in the House and is seeking a…
articles.body:
Sen. Ed Markey has fended off a challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton in the Massachusetts Democratic primary for Senate, Decision Desk HQ projects.

Moulton, a 47-year-old who’s served in the House for six terms, had lodged a generational change campaign against Markey, an 80-year-old who served 20 terms in the House and is seeking a third term in the Senate.

DDHQ called the race for Markey with just 4 percent of the vote reported. He led Moulton by over 30 percentage points as of 8:32 p.m. EDT.

But Markey emerged victorious in Tuesday’s primary, teeing him up for another six years representing the solidly blue state in the upper chamber alongside fellow Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.). He will face off against Republican John Deaton, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary, in November.

The results are in line with recent polls that showed the senator with a double-digit lead. A University of Massachusetts Amherst/WCVB poll in mid-August found the incumbent was backed by more than 4 in 5 likely Democratic primary voters, signaling that Markey’s age “may actually be advantageous” as voters labeled him progressive, experienced and trustworthy.

The primary was one of several this cycle in which younger challengers have targeted longtime Democratic lawmakers as conversations about health, age and term limits circulate within the party.

Former President Biden’s exit from the 2024 race amid health concerns and the recent passing of multiple congressional Democrats in office have invigorated younger candidates who argue that older lawmakers are out-of-touch with the party.

But unlike some high-profile contests that saw the younger challengers running to the left of the incumbents, Markey was seen by many as the more progressive in the race.

Warren, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) were among those who supported his bid — while The Boston Globe had endorsed Moulton, suggesting that the younger candidate could bring “new vision and vigor” to an “aging” Democratic Party.

Markey’s victory comes after he fended off a 2020 challenge from former Rep. Joe Kennedy III (D-Mass.), defeating his rival by roughly 10 percentage points in the primary and marking the first time a Kennedy family member lost a statewide race in Massachusetts.

articles.title: 80-year-old Dem beats back generational challenge after going all-in on trans athletes
articles.summary: Ed Markey defeated Seth Moulton's generational change campaign by leaning into progressive credentials and taking a bold stance on transgender rights in sports.
articles.body: One of the only Democrats stumping for transgender rights on the campaign trail fought back a younger challenger pushing generational change in the Senate. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., withstood a challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., to again be crowned as Massachusetts’ Democratic nominee for Senate in his quest for a third full term on Tuesday night. The Associated Press projected Markey would defeat Moulton less than an hour after polls closed. Markey, who has represented Massachusetts in Congress for nearly five decades, survived Moulton’s campaign focused on generational change by leaning into his progressive bona fides. Notably, he is one of the few Democrats running this midterm cycle who is continuing to push for transgender rights, particularly in sports. TOP 5 MOST HEATED MOMENTS AS PROGRESSIVES SPAR OVER WHO IS FURTHER TO THE LEFT IN FINAL DEM SENATE DEBATE "Trans athletes should be able to play," Markey told The New York Times. "That reflects Massachusetts and who we are. And Seth Moulton does not." The position, which has been used by Republicans as a political rallying cry on the campaign trail and one that Democrats have largely remained quiet about as they push to flip both chambers of Congress, is one that Moulton argued played a major factor in Democrats’ losing across the board in 2024. "I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that," Moulton said at the time. DEMOCRATS STAY QUIET ON NEXT STEPS AFTER SUPREME COURT TRANSGENDER SPORTS RULING Given Massachusetts’ position as a deep-blue bastion — the Bay State hasn’t had a Republican senator since 2013; former Sen. Scott Brown lost to Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass. — it’s unlikely that Markey’s position will cost him in November. And his primary victory marks another win for progressives. Markey, who co-authored the Green New Deal resolution years ago, boasted the backing of progressive titans, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. WATCH: LAWMAKERS REVEAL WHERE THEY STAND ON CONGRESSIONAL TERM LIMITS AFTER RECENT HEALTH SCARES It also serves as a blow to a broader push among Democrats across the country looking for generational change, particularly after the tumult that followed former President Joe Biden and his attempt to run for a second term in the White House. Though longtime incumbents have been defeated, including Rep. John Larson, D-Conn., 78, by the much younger Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, 47, Markey was able to hold on despite Moulton making age a key factor in his campaign. For his own part, Moulton, after losing the primary on Tuesday evening, said he viewed his campaign as a necessary challenge to even the party's most tenured figures. "Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary. I will continue to push the Democratic Party — and our country — to look towards the future," Moulton said in a statement. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Markey’s victory over Moulton isn’t the first time that a younger candidate has stepped into the arena only to be felled by the octogenarian. Markey bested Massachusetts political royalty in 2020, beating former Rep. Joe Kennedy III in a primary contest that, like his contentious battle against Moulton, centered on a changing of the guard in the upper chamber.

articles.body:
Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey (D) is projected to face off against Republican Mike Minogue in her quest for a second term as the Bay State’s top executive, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Healey ran unopposed in Tuesday’s Democratic primary while Minogue defeated Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority acting general manager Brian Shortsleeve in the GOP contest.

Minogue beat Shortsleeve by over 30 percentage points with 4 percent of the reported by DDHQ as of 8:49 p.m. EDT.

Minogue, the former CEO of Abiomed, faces an uphill battle to defeat Healey in November.

Cook Political Report rates the seat as solidly in Democrats’ corner.

Healey previously served as the state’s attorney general, and she is a staunch critic of President Trump. She easily won her first election for governor in 2022, defeating Republican opponent Geoff Diehl by nearly 30 percentage points.

She is the first woman to serve in the role in Massachusetts and only one of two openly lesbian candidates to win a gubernatorial election in U.S. history.

articles.title: Self-funded CEO claims GOP nomination to challenge Massachusetts Democrat’s second-term bid
articles.summary: Mike Minogue won 70% at the Massachusetts GOP convention and defeated former MBTA executive Brian Shortsleeve to take on Gov. Maura Healey.
articles.body: Former medical device executive Mike Minogue won the Massachusetts gubernatorial primary Tuesday, defeating Brian Shortsleeve, a former executive at the MBTA, the state-run transit agency. The winner will now face favored Democratic Gov. Maura Healey, who is running for a second term. Massachusetts has had continuous Democratic representation in Congress since 1996, but Republicans have had considerably more success in races for the governor's mansion since the Reagan era. Minogue emphasized his business credentials in campaign materials, citing his work at GE Healthcare before leading Danvers-based Abiomed. GOP GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE FIGHTING TO FLIP BLUE STATE UNVEILS HEALTHCARE PLAN TO LOWER COSTS, EXPAND ACCESS Minogue said that, while he was at Abiomed, the company developed the world’s smallest heart pump and doubled the size of its headquarters, increasing its in-state capabilities and creating jobs. Minogue also drew attention on social media when Boston-based Canadian American investor Kevin O’Leary, better known as Shark Tank’s "Mr. Wonderful," appeared in one of his videos and said he does not usually "show for politicians." "Massachusetts is ‘dead-money’ now. We need a guy like this to run the show," O’Leary said in July. TRUMP KEEPS WINNING REPUBLICAN PRIMARIES; HIS LOSSES MAY BE MORE REVEALING According to The Boston Herald, Healey launched a last-minute ad attacking Minogue as "MAGA Mike," which the newspaper said shows the executive "has Healey’s attention" and may help Shortsleeve. Minogue won the state’s GOP convention endorsement with 70% of the vote, while Shortsleeve earned his ballot position with a fraction of a percentage point more than the required 15%, according to reports. Minogue self-funded roughly $7 million of the more than $7.5 million he raised in the first quarter, hosted a fundraiser with Vice President JD Vance and has donated to Trump and the RNC. Shortsleeve raised about $646,500 in the first quarter of 2026. Healey was formally renominated Tuesday after running unopposed. Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll, a fellow Democrat, also advances unopposed to the November election. Republicans, however, have no candidates in about half of the state’s congressional districts or in the races for secretary of state and state auditor. A signature problem has forced lieutenant gubernatorial candidate Anne Manning Martin to run a write-in campaign. The district in the Berkshires, the district covering much of the Massachusetts Turnpike corridor, and two exurban Boston-area districts to the north and west have no Republican candidates competing Tuesday, guaranteeing Democratic nominees will advance in those races ahead of November. Massachusetts state government has not always been as reliably Democratic in modern times despite the conditions in this year’s contests. Former Gov. Charlie Baker, a moderate Republican, preceded Healey from 2015 to 2023. Former Sen. Mitt Romney, R-Utah, served as Massachusetts governor from 2003 to 2007 and opted against re-election before launching an unsuccessful presidential bid against President Barack Obama. Swift was elevated to the office when Cellucci became then-President George W. Bush's ambassador to Canada. Weld was preceded by 1988 Democratic presidential nominee Gov. Michael Dukakis, and Democrats more often held the governor’s office in the preceding era.

articles.title: GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts and independent Dan Osborn clash in fiery Nebraska Senate debate
articles.summary: Ricketts derided Osborn as a Democrat in all but name. Osborn said Ricketts isn’t representing Nebraska as they compete in a race on the fringe of the Senate battlefield.
articles.body: Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., went on offense against independent opponent Dan Osborn in a debate Tuesday night, repeatedly calling him “Democrat Dan” throughout their meeting and associating his campaign with democratic socialists. The debate will be the first of many across the country over the next two months as Democrats and Republicans battle for control of the Senate. Deep-red Nebraska is not usually home to nationally watched campaigns, but Osborn’s one-on-one contest with Ricketts could be closer than typical partisan contests in the state. This debate, which took place at the Nebraska State Fair, may be the only clash between the two candidates with nine weeks to go until Election Day. Osborn spent most of the debate distancing himself from both parties, but he was also careful not to completely cut ties with either side. The Democratic nominee in the Senate race, Cindy Burbank, dropped out this summer, and the state Democratic Party chair said she was supporting Osborn. Osborn ran in 2024 and lost to GOP Sen. Deb Fischer by less than 7 percentage points even as Donald Trump carried the state by 20 points. “I don’t need to caucus with either party,” Osborn said. “Nobody’s got a monopoly on a good idea. I will work with Republicans to get things passed, but it’s about delivering for Nebraska. That’s what I intend to do, is to work for the people of Nebraska, not a party boss.” Ricketts drew stark differences between himself and his opponent, attacking Osborn over his support for “Medicare for All” and saying Osborn would not have supported the tax cuts and other measures in Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.” “Yes, I would have voted against the state that the current Big Beautiful Bill Act is in,” Osborn said. “But since we’re delving in hypotheticals, that act was passed by a tiebreaker for JD Vance. So if I would have beaten Deb Fischer and operated as a true independent in Washington, D.C., that would have been leverage. That would have been leverage to deliver for Nebraska.” One of the major themes throughout the debate was PAC spending in both campaigns, as well as “dark money” coming from unidentified donors. Ricketts called out his opponent several times about his campaign finances, saying that his top fundraising sources were Washington, D.C., New York and California and that he’d gotten funds from top Democrats like Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. “Democrat Dan keeps trying to insinuate that somehow I can be part of this billionaires club or whatever,” Ricketts said. “The truth is I can’t be bought. He already has. He’s been paid for by those liberal out-of-state interests who are funding his campaign.” After having mentioned several times throughout the debate that “dark money” is a problem in the election system that needs a fix, Osborn admitted that he has benefited from secret donors who have given to outside groups supporting his campaign. “I don’t know who these people are, and they raise money in my name, and those are the ones that run ads,” Osborn said. “If it doesn’t say ‘I’m Dan Osborn’ or ‘I’m Pete Ricketts, I approve this message,’ that’s dark money working.” The debate was broken into three parts, each individually focusing on tariffs and the cost of living, ICE and the war in Iran, and campaign financing and artificial intelligence.

articles.body: President Donald Trump announced Tuesday that he is nominating acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao to permanently lead the service, calling the former Navy special operations officer a "true WARRIOR" and urging the Senate to quickly confirm him. Cao has served as acting secretary for the past four months, overseeing the Navy and Marine Corps as the Trump administration pushes to expand U.S. shipbuilding and strengthen the military’s maritime capabilities. "I am pleased to nominate a true WARRIOR, Hung Cao, to become the next Secretary of the Navy," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "We need Patriots like Hung leading our Navy and Marine Corps, and I can think of no one better than him to make sure our Great Navy and Marine Corps remain the FIERCEST and BEST Force the World has ever seen," the president continued. TRUMP PRAISES OUSTED NAVY SECRETARY PHELAN AMID TENSIONS WITH PENTAGON LEADERSHIP Trump called on the Senate to move quickly on the nomination, pointing to Cao’s tenure already leading the department. SENATE REPUBLICANS CONFIRM NEARLY 50 OF TRUMP'S PICKS FOR ENERGY, LAND MANAGEMENT "The Senate needs to confirm this Warfighter, ASAP, so he can continue the fantastic work he has been doing over the past 4 months," Trump wrote. Cao is a retired Navy captain who served for 25 years in uniform after graduating from the U.S. Naval Academy. articles.title: House Democrat survives left-flank challenge as Bernie volunteer mounts insurgent bid
articles.summary: Jake Auchincloss advanced against progressive challenger Jason Poulos, who campaigned on Medicare-for-all and ending U.S. military aid to Israel.
articles.body: Rep. Jake Auchincloss advanced Tuesday against Jason Poulos in Massachusetts’ 4th Congressional District. Auchincloss has held his seat since 2021 and faced his first Democratic primary challenge since winning the seat. Progressive challenger Poulos is an AI policy researcher who has been critical of Auchincloss regarding past support for military aid to Israel and ties to AIPAC while calling for an end to U.S. military assistance to Israel. PROGRESSIVE WAVE CRASHES IN SUN BELT BATTLEGROUND AS MODERATE HOLDS HIS SEAT Poulos, who previously volunteered for Bernie Sanders’ campaign, ran on Medicare-for-all, universal basic income, taxes on corporate automation, stronger unions and student debt cancellation. He also wanted to reduce military spending and end U.S. military aid to Israel. While Auchincloss is endorsed by AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, he has been critical of aspects of Israel's conduct in Gaza by saying some Israeli actions in 2025 "crossed lines" on humanitarian conditions. AIPAC is an influential pro-Israel lobbying group that has been criticized for advocating for U.S. military aid to Israel amid the war in Gaza. HOUSE DEMOCRATS FRACTURE BADLY OVER MASSIE AMENDMENT TO CUT $3.3B IN U.S. AID TO ISRAEL In July, Auchincloss voted with more than 100 House Democrats to eliminate $3.3 billion in U.S. military financing for Israel, while maintaining his support for the U.S.-Israel alliance. Auchincloss campaigned on lowering housing and healthcare costs, promoting economic growth and positioning Democrats to better confront the economic disruption caused by AI. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Auchincloss, who succeeded Joe Kennedy III, comes from a prominent Boston medical family. He had previously been a registered Republican and worked on former Gov. Charlie Baker’s campaign, a line his primary opponents used against him. He later returned to the Democratic Party.

articles.title: Top Democrat survives double-barreled challenge as party’s Israel divide hits home
articles.summary: House Minority Whip Katherine Clark advanced past two left-wing challengers who made Gaza and AIPAC money central issues in the Democratic primary.
articles.body: House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark toppled two progressive challengers Tuesday in Massachusetts' safely Democratic 5th Congressional District, surviving a primary fight that put Gaza and pro-Israel political spending at the center of the race. Clark, who won handily Tuesday night against fellow Democratic Party contenders Jonathan Paz and Tarik Samman, was first elected in 2013 during a special election and has held her position as House Democratic whip since 2022. The second-highest ranking Democrat after House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Clark has helped lead opposition to Republican spending, immigration and healthcare measures, including recent messaging against ICE funding and GOP cuts to Head Start and Medicaid. MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 MIDTERMS She ran against former city councilor, educator and union organizer Paz and 27-year-old Harvard Law School researcher and union organizer Samman. Clark fended off two left-wing challengers who sought to make Gaza and pro-Israel political money central issues in the safely blue Boston-area primary. Her fundraising operation dwarfed both challengers, raising $4.5 million, while Paz raised $88,500 and Samman brought in $43,800, according to FEC filings. PELOSI-BACKED DEMOCRAT LOSES AFTER $10M FLOOD OF CRYPTO, PRO-ISRAEL MONEY While AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, endorsed Clark and has contributed to her campaign in the past, she has taken a critical stance toward the Israeli government’s handling of the war in Gaza. AIPAC is an influential pro-Israel lobbying group that has been criticized for advocating for U.S. military aid to Israel amid the war in Gaza. Last year, Clark used the word "genocide" at a district event before clarifying that she was not accusing Israel of genocide. Then, in July, she voted to cut $3.3 billion in U.S. military aid, saying Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government had failed to meet U.S. interests and values. Clark has continued to support Israel as a sovereign Jewish state and backed U.S. assistance for some Israeli defensive systems but is critical of Netanyahu. TOP HOUSE DEMOCRAT SAYS ANTI-ISRAEL ACTIVISTS’ THREATS KEPT HIM FROM TOWN HALLS FOR A YEAR Samman and Paz have argued that while Clark has increasingly criticized Israel’s conduct in Gaza, she has yet to renounce the AIPAC money she has accepted. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Clark ran unopposed in 2024. Her most recent general election opponent was Republican Caroline Colarusso, whom Clark defeated 74% to 26% in 2022.

articles.title: Former Biden official wins primary for open Moulton House seat in Massachusetts
articles.summary: Democrat Daniel Koh is projected to win his party’s primary for the House seat left open by Rep. Seth Moulton (D), according to Decision Desk HQ. Koh was locked in a tough primary battle against progressive state Rep. Tram Nguyen for the seat representing the state’s 6th Congressional District. Moulton, who has represented the district…
articles.body:
Democrat Daniel Koh is projected to win his party’s primary for the House seat left open by Rep. Seth Moulton (D), according to Decision Desk HQ.

Koh was locked in a tough primary battle against progressive state Rep. Tram Nguyen for the seat representing the state’s 6th Congressional District. Moulton, who has represented the district for a decade, opted to leave his seat and challenge Sen. Ed Markey (D).

He led Nguyen by 10 percentage points with 68 percent of the vote reported Tuesday evening — nearly 41 to about 30 percent — per DDHQ.

Four other candidates were on the Tuesday ballot, including veterinarian Mariah Lancaster who dropped out over the weekend and endorsed Nguyen.

A White House official under President Biden, Koh notched high-profile endorsements from the former president as well as former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, among others. Nguyen received support from Democratic Massachusetts Reps. Lori Trahan and Ayanna Pressley as well as The Boston Globe.

Koh is almost certain to win the blue seat representing the northeastern portion of the state. He will face off against Republican Micah Jones, a lawyer and Army veteran, who ran unopposed for the GOP nod.

In 2018, Koh ran in Massachusett’s 3rd Congressional District, losing to Trahan. He previously served as shief of staff for Boston Mayor Marty Walsh.

The mayor later became Labor secretary under Biden before resigning to run the National Hockey League Players’ Association. Koh served as Walsh’s chief of staff in Washington before joining the White House’s Office of Intergovernmental Affairs.

articles.title: Biden-Harris favorite gets second shot at Congress, beats Squad-backed candidate
articles.summary: Dan Koh, backed by Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, won a crowded Democratic primary for the House seat Seth Moulton is vacating in Massachusetts.
articles.body: A former Biden administration aide just won a crowded primary race in Massachusetts, setting up a glide path to the House of Representatives come November. Dan Koh came out first among six candidates to replace Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., who ended his House tenure with a failed run for Senate against incumbent Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., that came to a conclusion Tuesday night. Koh had the backing of both former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris, which was no surprise after his stint working in the White House. He first joined the administration as chief of staff to then-Labor Secretary Marty Walsh and later became deputy assistant to the president and deputy director of the White House Office of Intergovernmental Affairs. BIDEN INTERVENES IN DEM CONGRESSIONAL PRIMARY, WARNING ALL 'WE DID TO HELP ORDINARY PEOPLE IS IN JEOPARDY NOW' But his successful Tuesday primary is not the first time Koh ran for Congress. He narrowly lost the Democratic nomination in Massachusetts' nearby 3rd Congressional District to Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., in 2018. Koh is running on progressive campaign promises like abolishing "Trump's ICE" referring to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and universal healthcare. He's now poised to succeed Moulton in the 6th Congressional District, which includes the northeastern portion of Massachusetts and is rated a safe blue seat. HARRIS-BACKED DEMOCRAT SCRUBS BLM-ERA POSTS AS HOUSE CAMPAIGN HEATS UP Moulton, who served in the Marine Corps, has represented the district since 2015. His campaign for Senate has been marked by a bitter primary battle against Markey, an 80-year-old progressive who has been in office since 2013. Moulton, 47, ran his campaign based on generational change and arguing that Markey had long missed his chance to substantively make life better for Massachusetts residents, but that wasn't enough to stave him off Tuesday. AOC ENDORSES SEN ED MARKEY AS INCUMBENT FACES DEM US SENATE PRIMARY CHALLENGE FROM REP SETH MOULTON Markey is backed by the far left's marquee names, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. Meanwhile, Koh himself is a figure of the establishment left, with both his father and uncle also serving in the federal government. His father, Howard Koh, was an assistant secretary in the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) under former President Barack Obama. His uncle served under the Obama and Clinton administrations. articles.title: Lynch fends off Massachusetts House primary challenge in battle over generational change

articles.body:
Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.) is projected to fend off a primary challenge from his left and defeat attorney Patrick Roath in a battle defined by generational change, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Lynch, 71, defeated Roath, 39, in the Democratic primary for Massachusetts’s 8th Congressional District. Roath, who served as an aide to former Gov. Deval Patrick (D), was the only Democrat challenging the incumbent.

The incumbent is poised to win by about 15 percentage points with 47 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ Tuesday evening.

Lynch’s win is notable given seven House Democrats lost their primaries in a cycle defined by calls for generational change within the party. An anti-establishment and anti-incumbent energy that has dominated this primary season on both sides of the aisle.

On the campaign trail, Roath hammered the congressman, who’s served in the lower chamber since 2001, over several of his past votes, including against former President Obama’s signature healthcare package in 2010 and for the Laken Riley Act.

Lynch argued that he had delivered results for the 8th Congressional District and pointed to his for the DREAM Act when it was politically unpopular. He said his background and upbringing was emblematic of those who lived in the district as someone who grew up in public housing in South Boston.

Lynch’s win demonstrates the limits to which younger, progressive challengers can topple longtime incumbents — even in a favorable political environment.

Several other primaries centered around generational change and age are also playing out in Massachusetts on Tuesday: Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.) is primarying Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) for Markey’s Senate seat and high school teacher Jeromie Whalen is primarying Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.) in the western 1st Congressional District.

articles.title: Rep. Stephen Lynch outpaces 39-year-old challenger in Massachusetts House District 8 Democratic primary
articles.summary: Lynch won against Patrick Roath, NBC News projects, who is more than three decades younger and came at him from the left.
articles.body: Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch has defeated a younger, more progressive primary challenger, NBC News projects, in the highest-profile test remaining for House incumbents after a turbulent primary season. Lynch, 71, won renomination over Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old former aide to former Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick. With his win, Lynch staved off an attempt to add him to the list of Democratic officeholders dethroned by rivals pushing for generational change. Elsewhere in the state, fellow veteran Democratic Rep. Richard Neal also secured renomination, defeating teacher Jeromie Whalen in another Democratic primary. On the other side of Massachusetts, Roath outraised Lynch, outspent him significantly on the airwaves and scored The Boston Globe editorial board’s endorsement to go with backing from Patrick, progressive activist David Hogg’s group, Leaders We Deserve, and key teachers unions. That support helped Roath press Lynch for months in one of the toughest fights of his political career. He highlighted Lynch’s various breaks with his party in the past, including votes against the Affordable Care Act and, more recently, for the Laken Riley Act. Roath also called for progressive measures like “Medicare for All,” abolishing ICE and restricting military aid to Israel. But Lynch persevered, trumpeting work that he says held the Trump administration accountable and leaning on his decades of experience, including deep relationships with unions and other fixtures in the district. “I got to know this district by living here and regularly attending hundreds of town meetings, not just to speak, but to listen and understand the needs and priorities of the people that I represent,” Lynch said at an August forum sponsored by the League of Women Voters Hingham and others. He touted “tens of billions of dollars that I’ve been able to bring back to our district” and added that he “accomplished much of that as a member of the minority party in Congress. You can only imagine what we can do together if the situation changes.” Lynch’s victory means he has avoided the fate of 11 of his House colleagues — including seven Democrats — who lost primary challenges this year as voters took some of their frustrations with Washington out on incumbent lawmakers. Another two senators, both Republicans whose primary opponents got Trump endorsements, also lost primaries this year. Neal also avoided defeat in another primary marked by arguments over generational change and progressive policy proposals. Whalen, 39, a high school teacher, ran a campaign decrying the “old-school political entanglements that got us into this mess” and called to abolish ICE and cut off U.S. military aid to Israel. Neal spent more than $1 million on campaign ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, about 10 times what Whalen spent. Meanwhile, in the open 6th District, Dan Koh won the Democratic primary in the race to succeed Rep. Seth Moulton, who ran for the Senate but lost that primary to Sen. Ed Markey. Koh was an aide to a variety of top Democrats, including former Boston Mayor Marty Walsh, and chief of staff of the U.S. Labor Department, and he was the top fundraiser in the race. Both former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris have appeared in an ad for Koh, who has emphasized that he wants to take on Trump and his “corruption,” calling to abolish ICE and pass “Medicare for All.”

articles.title: One of Congress' most powerful Democrats just survived a progressive primary revolt
articles.summary: Richard Neal defeated progressive challenger Jeromie Whalen in the Massachusetts 1st Congressional District primary, but the seniority debate rages on.
articles.body: The progressive push to unseat a veteran Democratic power broker fell short Tuesday, when Rep. Richard Neal defeated high school teacher Jeromie Whalen in Massachusetts' 1st Congressional District primary. Neal, 77, has represented western Massachusetts in Congress for nearly four decades and has built considerable influence as the top Democrat on the powerful tax-writing House Ways and Means Committee. His 39-year-old challenger ran on a platform that included Medicare for All, higher taxes on the wealthy, abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and a pledge to reject campaign contributions from corporate PACs. The race tested whether progressive voters were ready to replace a longtime Democratic incumbent, even if it meant giving up the clout Neal’s seniority brings western Massachusetts. 2026 MIDTERMS: PRIMARIES, KEY RACES AND ELECTION RESULTS Whalen sought to cast Neal as a representative of the Democratic establishment unwilling to take on wealthy interests and corporate power, while pitching himself as part of a younger generation pushing the party further to the left. Neal, meanwhile, made his experience and position in Washington central to his case for re-election, arguing that his seniority gives the district influence in Congress that would be difficult for a first-term lawmaker to replicate. The contest also unfolded against a broader debate inside the Democratic Party over its aging leadership and whether longtime incumbents should step aside for a younger generation. Progressive stalwart Sen. Ed Markey, 80, defeated a more moderate challenger 33 years his junior on Tuesday night. MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 Neal's position on the Ways and Means Committee also gave the race significance beyond western Massachusetts. The panel sits at the center of congressional fights over taxes and other major economic policy. His victory also ultimately preserves the seat of one of the House Democratic caucus' most senior members while turning back a challenge built around the argument that the party needs generational and ideological change. articles.title: Markey shrugs off Moulton in generational clash: 3 takeaways from Massachusetts primaries
articles.summary: Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) bucked this cycle’s recent trend of old guard Democrats losing primaries to younger challengers, easily routing his rival in Tuesday’s primary for Senate in Massachusetts. The race was the latest test of Democrats’ appetite for generational change in Congress – but with a progressive incumbent against a more moderate challenger, it featured a flipped dynamic compared to other high-profile showdowns…
articles.body:
Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) bucked this cycle’s recent trend of old guard Democrats losing primaries to younger challengers, easily routing his rival in Tuesday’s primary for Senate in Massachusetts.

The race was the latest test of Democrats’ appetite for generational change in Congress – but with a progressive incumbent against a more moderate challenger, it featured a flipped dynamic compared to other high-profile showdowns this year.

At the same time, a pair of longtime moderate House Democrats also prevailed against younger, more progressive rivals on Tuesday, defying one of the defining trends of this primary cycle.

A string of other primaries in the solidly blue state, which appeared to spark strong turnout numbers , also solidified Moulton’s successor and set the stage in several contested primaries for district attorney.

Here are the key takeaways from Tuesday’s races:

The Democratic primary for Senate in Massachusetts offered dueling visions of change for the party. And Bay Staters stuck with the status quo.

Moulton, a 47-year-old who’s served six House terms, unsuccesfully pitches his younger perspective, while Markey, an 80-year-old who’s been on Capitol Hill for five decades, touted his progressive action.

With roughly 71 percent of the vote in as of 11:15 p.m. EDT on Tuesday, the incumbent was ahead of Moulton by nearly 30 percentage points.

Amid ongoing debate in the party about age, health and term limits for long-serving lawmakers, Markey’s credentials outweighed his status as the oldest Senate Democrat running for reelection.

Unlike other primaries this cycle — in which younger, progressive rivals sought to oust more centrist Democratic incumbents — Moulton was seen as relatively moderate candidate. And while blue lawmakers in other states have consistently lost to political newcomers, Moulton was running with more than a decade of experience on Capitol Hill.

Polling ahead of the race suggested the incumbent had a double-digit advantage over Moulton, with some indications that his progressive record was a boost, despite critiques over his age. He also had support from progressive titans, including Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.).

Moulton, on the other hand, called for “a new generation of leadership,” while some supporters also pushed back on his characterization as more moderate. When Markey appeared to struggle on a debate question about artificial intelligence, Moulton argued it was a sign for younger voices to weigh in on tech and other pressing issues.

Regardless, Tuesday’s results mark an easy win for Markey after he defeated former Rep. Joe Kennedy III (D-Mass.) in a 2020 primary, marking the first time a Kennedy family member lost a statewide race in Massachusetts.

Former Obama strategist David Axelrod on Tuesday hailed Markey’s victory “despite his age, because, in his Golden Years, he’s grabbed on to the Green New Deal, Medicare for All, trans rights and other marquee priorities of the Left,” despite starting out in Congress as a social conservative.

“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary. I will continue to push the Democratic Party — and our country — to look towards the future,” Moulton said in a statement on the results. He pledged to “do everything I can” to help re-elect Markey in November.

“We didn’t achieve our goal tonight, but I am confident that because of this campaign others will be inspired to buck the system when they’re told to ‘wait their turn.’”

Alongside Markey, two other veteran Democrats on Capitol Hill warded off younger rivals in a pair of deep blue House races.

Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.), a 71-year-old running for a 14th term in the House, defeated 39-year-old attorney Patrick Roath, all but assuring he’ll hold on to his Boston-area seat in the 8th district.

Roath, backed by David Hogg’s Leaders We Deserve organization, told The Hill this week that “even people who have supported Stephen Lynch for two decades are ready for change.”

Unlike Markey in the Senate contest, Lynch is considered a relative moderate, but he was leading by around 15 points when the race was called around 11:15 p.m., with 61 of the vote in.

Over in the western Massachusetts 1st district, Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), who at 77 has served in the House for 19 terms, also beat back 39-year-old public school teacher Jeromie Whalen in his Democratic primary.

Whalen stressed that he was running because of corporate influence in elections but also highlighted that he’s half of the incumbent’s age.

When the race was called around 11:15 p.m.. on Tuesday, Neal was leading Whalen by about 11 points, with 72 percent of the vote in.

This year’s races are shadowed by the passing of multiple lawmakers in office, as well as renewed concerns about health and age amid 84-year-old Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) prolonged absence from Capitol Hill — and the fallout from President Biden’s surprise exit from the 2024 race amid critiques of his fitness for office.

The median age of voting members in the House was 57.5 years at the start of the 119 th Congress, according to Pew Research analysis last year. More than two-thirds of the body were aged 50 or older, and just 36 members in the 435-seat House were under age 40.

The median age in the Senate was 64.7 years at the start of this Congress, with two-thirds of the 100-member body age 60 or older, and just 2 members under age 40.

The moderate in the Democratic primary to succeed Moulton in northeastern Massachusetts came out on top Tuesday.

Former White House staffer Dan Koh is on the fast track to join Congress after beating a crowded field of Democrats, including progressive state Rep. Tram Nguyen and four other candidates, in the solid blue 6 t h district.

Koh had some of the biggest names in Democratic politics in his corner. Former President Biden as well as former Vice President Harris and Biden-era Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg all threw their weight behind his candidacy.

Before joining the White House’s Office of Intergovernmental Affairs under Biden, he served as Labor Secretary Marty Walsh’s chief of staff. He was also Walsh’s top aide when he served as Boston mayor.

Nguyen, meanwhile, secured the backing of The Boston Globe and Progressive Massachusetts as well as Democratic Reps. Lori Trahan and Ayanna Pressley, who both ran unopposed in their Tuesday primaries.

Koh held a huge fundraising advantage over Nguyen too — securing over $4.7 million in contributions, per the Federal Elections Commission. Nguyen raised just under $895,000.

Koh first ran for Congress in 2018, losing to Trahan in the 3 rd district in razor-thin primary after requesting a recount, according to the Associated Press .

A Republican has not held the 6 th district seat since 1997. Koh will face off against Republican Micah Jones this fall.
